query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The apparently disconnected strength, creep, hardness, elastic-modulus and thermal-expansion data for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr arise from temperature-dependent formation and dissolution of nanoscale chemical short-range order (SRO)—B2/ω-like ordered clusters—inside its b.c.c. solid-solution matrix. When SRO is present (≈600–1000 °C or after deformation-induced clustering) it stiffens the lattice and impedes dislocation motion, raising hardness, flow stress and elastic modulus; when SRO dissolves above ≈1000 °C the lattice softens, permitting the high creep rates observed at 1250 °C. Differential thermal expansion between ordered clusters and the disordered matrix produces internal stresses that modify the measured coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE).
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenised, single-phase b.c.c. equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy cast ingot.
generation.intervention: Generate contrasting SRO levels by (i) aging at 700 °C for 72 h followed by water quench to freeze in SRO ("SRO-rich" condition) versus (ii) solution-treating at 1400 °C for 1 h followed by water quench to maximise chemical disorder ("SRO-poor" baseline).
generation.conditions: All subsequent tests in flowing Ar: (a) room-temperature microhardness and nanoindentation, (b) dynamic Young’s modulus and linear thermal-expansion measurements from 293–1100 K at 5 K min⁻¹, (c) constant-stress tensile creep at 1250 °C, 150 MPa for 50 h.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale B2/ω-like chemically ordered clusters (short-range order) within the b.c.c. matrix, whose volume fraction decreases sharply above ~1000 K.
generation.mechanism: Ordered clusters produce local lattice stiffening and strong elastic misfit that (1) raise modulus, (2) block dislocation glide (hardening during cold work or aging), and (3) create CTE mismatch stresses; dissolution of clusters at high T removes these barriers, lowering modulus and enabling rapid dislocation climb that governs the fast creep seen at 1250 °C.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the SRO-poor baseline, the SRO-rich alloy will exhibit: 1) ≈10–20 % higher room-temperature hardness and yield stress; 2) ≈5–10 % higher Young’s modulus below 800 K, followed by a marked (≥5 %) drop between 900–1000 K as SRO dissolves; 3) a kink (change in slope) in the CTE curve in the same 900–1000 K range; 4) an initial steady-state creep rate at 1250 °C at least two-fold lower during the first ~10 h, converging to the baseline rate as ordering is lost.
generation.baseline: Solution-treated (1400 °C/1 h, water-quenched) HfNbTaTiZr with minimal SRO.
generation.boundary: Effects are significant only while ordered clusters are stable (≈600–1000 °C). Below ~500 °C or above ~1100 °C both states converge in modulus, hardness and creep response.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude and stability range of SRO in this specific HEA are inferred from analogous refractory alloys; if actual ordering is weaker or dissolves at lower temperature, predicted differences may be smaller or absent.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare SRO-rich and SRO-poor specimens as described. (1) Use synchrotron or neutron total scattering with pair-distribution-function analysis at room T, 800 K and 1100 K to quantify SRO. (2) Measure dynamic modulus (resonant ultrasound) and dilatometry during continuous heating 293–1100 K. (3) Record Vickers hardness and nanoindentation modulus at room temperature. (4) Conduct constant-stress tensile creep at 1250 °C/150 MPa, measuring strain vs time for 50 h.
measurements: Intensity and position of PDF peaks characteristic of B2/ω SRO
Coefficient of thermal expansion vs temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if (a) PDF shows no greater SRO in aged specimens, OR (b) modulus and CTE curves of both states are identical within ±2 %, OR (c) hardness differs by <5 %, OR (d) steady-state creep rates at 1250 °C differ by <10 % for the first 10 h.
